title: Fifty Hours on a Toilet to Fund Who Gives A Crap's First Run
dek: In July 2012 Simon Griffiths sat on a toilet on a live webcam in Melbourne until strangers had pre-ordered $50,000 of recycled toilet paper.

story.founder: Simon Griffiths, Jehan Ratnatunga, Danny Alexander
story.event: Sitting on a toilet on a livestream until crowdfunding pre-orders reached $50,000
story.summary: On 10 July 2012 Simon Griffiths, co-founder of Who Gives A Crap with Jehan Ratnatunga and Danny Alexander, sat on a toilet in a Melbourne warehouse on a live webcam and pledged not to get up until the company's IndieGoGo campaign had pre-sold $50,000 of recycled toilet paper, half of whose profits were to go through WaterAid to build toilets. The target was reached after about 50 hours. The first product shipped in March 2013, and the company stayed self-funded apart from the crowdfunding until it raised $30 million in 2021.
paragraphs: On the morning of 10 July 2012, Simon Griffiths sat down on a toilet in his company's empty warehouse in Melbourne, in front of a live webcam, and said he would not get up until strangers had pre-ordered $50,000 of toilet paper. "I'm sitting down for what I believe in, and I'm not getting up till I've got some toilet paper," he said in the campaign video. He was 29, an engineering and economics graduate.

He, Jehan Ratnatunga and Danny Alexander had spent about two years developing the product: toilet paper made entirely from recycled paper, without chlorine, with half the profits to go through WaterAid towards toilets for people who had none. The founders had worked with humanitarian organisations; Griffiths also said the idea came partly from using disgusting toilets himself. What they lacked was money for a first bulk run of about 50,000 rolls, and any proof that people would buy toilet paper online. A crowdfunding campaign on IndieGoGo was meant to answer both at once, since every pledge was a pre-order.

The feed ran around the clock, so anyone could check he was not cheating. Griffiths could not sleep, and after the first day the sitting began to hurt, a Melbourne newspaper reported; messages of support arrived from as far away as Brazil, and a ski lodge in Japan gave $2,500. The first $50,000 came in some 50 hours after he sat down. By 12 July pledges had passed $53,000, and by 20 July just over $60,000. A later company profile says it took him three days to recover.

The first rolls were delivered in March 2013. According to that 2019 profile, the founders expected a slow start once the pre-orders were filled; instead sales doubled day on day, and what was meant to be three months of stock sold out in five days. Apart from the crowdfunding, the company was largely self-funded until 2021, when it raised $30 million from investors.

quote.text: Not nakedness, not platted hair, not dirt, not fasting, or lying on the earth, not rubbing with dust, not sitting motionless, can purify a mortal who has not overcome desires.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The Dhammapada says no display of endurance, sitting motionless included, purifies anyone by itself. Griffiths's fifty hours did what he needed and raised the money; the verse still asks whether, from the outside, a spectacle and the substance behind it can be told apart.

reflection: It is easy to remember the toilet and forget the two years before it. The stunt held attention for fifty hours. What kept customers afterwards was a product the founders had already spent two years getting right, and a plain promise about where half the profits would go.

The Dhammapada is blunt about displays of endurance: sitting still purifies no one on its own. That does not make the stunt wrong, but it puts it in its place. When you are tempted to prove your commitment by how long you can go without sleep or rest, it is fair to ask what the effort is actually carrying.
invitation: Before you push through one more late evening this week, write one line saying what the extra hours will actually produce. If you cannot name it, go home and rest instead.

cross_checks.claim: Griffiths began sitting on a toilet on live webcam on 10 July 2012, pledging to stay until IndieGoGo pledges reached $50,000
The $50,000 target was reached after about 50 hours (over two days)
The money was to pay for the first bulk production run
Half of profits were pledged through WaterAid to build toilets
The sit took place in Melbourne, in the team's warehouse

research_notes: Dating comes from contemporary coverage: Mumbrella published the launch on 10 July 2012 ('launches today'), TriplePundit (20 July 2012) says Griffiths sat down on the morning of 10 July and reached the milestone about 50 hours later, and HuffPost (12 July 2012) reported more than $53,000 by Thursday 12 July. The campaign's IndieGoGo page blocks automated requests and is not cited, so the story says only 'the morning of 10 July'. Duration: TriplePundit, CNBC and YPO say about 50 hours; GlobalPost says 'over two days'; these agree. Totals: HuffPost gave more than $53,000 on 12 July and TriplePundit just over $60,000 on 20 July; TriplePundit also says the company needed $100,000 in all, a figure no other source repeats, so the story gives the $50,000 sit target and the two dated totals only. Currency: YPO calls the target AUD 50,000; the 2012 reports just say $50,000; the story gives the figure without a currency label, as the reports did. Setting: HuffPost's headline says 'in his bathroom', while CNBC says the team's empty warehouse and GlobalPost says Melbourne; the story uses the warehouse. The details that he could not sleep and felt pain after the first day come from The Age as summarised by GlobalPost, so they are attributed to 'a Melbourne newspaper'. The World's page is dated 31 July 2016, but its text (Griffiths aged 29, image file dated 120712) shows it is a GlobalPost news-desk item from July 2012 carried over in a site migration. The three-day recovery, the 50,000-roll first run and the sell-out of three months' stock in five days rest on YPO's 2019 profile, which reflects the company's own account, and are attributed to it. CNBC does not say whether the $30 million raised in 2021 is in US or Australian dollars, so no currency is given. The Dhammapada verse is about ascetic practices as a path to purity and is applied here by analogy.
